## Goal

Distinguish representative sampling from precise repeated measurement; reverse
an extraction and dilution chain; calculate an ideal partition recovery; and
state which losses an added spike can test. Work by hand before using the demo
and R. All supplied datasets are simulated.

## Background

A heterogeneous solid has three equal-mass strata with mean iron concentrations
8, 14 and 25 mg/kg. Its bulk mass mean weights the strata by **mass**, not by the
number of convenient grabs. A composite can estimate a bulk quantity but no
longer preserves every original spatial difference.

For a caffeine extraction, the concentration in the measured flask must be
returned through aliquot and extract volumes to the original mass:

$$w_{extracted}=c_{final}\frac{V_{final}}{V_{aliquot}}
\frac{V_{extract}}{m_{sample}}.$$

Use litres for $V_{extract}$ when $c$ is mg/L. The result is **extracted caffeine**;
complete native-analyte recovery is not established. For ideal immiscible phases,
$D=c_o/c_a$ and the fraction remaining after n equal fresh extractions using total
solvent $V_o$ is $[V_a/(V_a+D V_o/n)]^n$.

## By hand

**B1.** Find the bulk mean of the three equal-mass strata. What mean would many
top-only grabs approach? Explain why a small SD would not fix this difference.
[Hint](#hint-b1)

**B2.** Instead suppose top, middle and bottom represent mass fractions 0.50,
0.30 and 0.20. Calculate the bulk mean. Why is an equal-stratum average now wrong?
[Hint](#hint-b2)

**B3.** A 0.5000 g dry portion gives 25.00 mL extract. A 2.00 mL aliquot made to
10.00 mL reads 1.92 mg caffeine/L. Calculate extract concentration, extracted
amount, and extracted caffeine in mg/g. [Hint](#hint-b3)

**B4.** At $D=9$ with 20 mL aqueous phase, compare recovery using one 10 mL
extraction with two fresh 5 mL extractions. State the physical assumptions.
[Hint](#hint-b4)

**B5.** A spike added after extraction gives the expected incremental response.
Does this establish complete recovery of native bound analyte? Explain which
parts of the measurement it did and did not experience. [Hint](#hint-b5)

## In R

Run from the course project's root. The raw dictionaries define sample and
preparation identities. In the grab table, rows are grabs within a specified
position. T1a and T1b are independent preparations of the same supplied material,
not independently collected materials.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
grabs <- read_csv("data/course/sampling.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
strata <- grabs |>
  group_by(position) |>
  summarise(n_grabs = n(), mean_mg_kg = mean(iron_mg_kg), .groups = "drop")
strata
mean(strata$mean_mg_kg)
prep <- read_csv("data/course/extractions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(prep$preparation_id), all(prep$mass_g > 0))
results <- prep |>
  mutate(extract_mg_l = final_caffeine_mg_l * final_ml / aliquot_ml,
         extracted_mg = extract_mg_l * extract_ml / 1000,
         caffeine_mg_g = extracted_mg / mass_g)
results
fig <- ggplot(results, aes(preparation_id, caffeine_mg_g)) + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Independent preparation", y = "Extracted caffeine (mg/g)") +
  theme_minimal()
fig
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(results, "output/extracted-caffeine.csv")
one_recovery <- 1 - 20 / (20 + 9 * 10)
two_recovery <- 1 - (20 / (20 + 9 * 5))^2
100 * c(one = one_recovery, two = two_recovery)
```

**R1.** Confirm B1, B3 and B4. Explain why `mean(grabs$iron_mg_kg)` happens to
give the same bulk result for this particular balanced table but is not a
universal sampling rule. [Hint](#hint-r1)

**R2.** Explain the unit conversion `/1000` and name the material basis of each
new results column. Which result would be wrong if you used measured final
concentration directly as mg/g? [Hint](#hint-r2)

**R3.** A new preparation uses 0.4000 g, 40.00 mL extract, and 1.00 mL made to
10.00 mL giving 1.50 mg/L. Add a calculation to your report and explain why the
result still needs a recovery qualification. [Hint](#hint-r3)

**R4.** Export the sampling experiment and save `sampling-demo.csv` at the
project root. Reproduce both averages when all strata are represented:

```r
if (file.exists("sampling-demo.csv")) {
  demo <- read_csv("sampling-demo.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
  print(mean(demo$iron_mg_kg))
  demo_strata <- demo |>
    group_by(stratum) |>
    summarise(mean_mg_kg = mean(iron_mg_kg), .groups = "drop")
  if (nrow(demo_strata) == 3) print(mean(demo_strata$mean_mg_kg))
}
```

Why does an absent stratum need to remain missing rather than being assigned
0 mg/kg? [Hint](#hint-r4)

## Hints

::: {#hint-b1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B1"}
For equal masses, average stratum means. Repeating a biased selection changes
random scatter but not the material left unsampled.
:::

::: {#hint-b2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B2"}
Multiply each concentration by its material mass fraction, then sum. Fractions
must refer to the intended target and add to one.
:::

::: {#hint-b3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B3"}
Undo the final dilution first, multiply by the total extract in litres, then
divide the extracted mg by original grams.
:::

::: {#hint-b4 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B4"}
For one extraction, the fraction left is $20/(20+9\times10)$. For two, multiply
the fraction left after each fresh 5 mL extraction.
:::

::: {#hint-b5 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B5"}
A late spike does not pass through earlier losses. Even an early freely dissolved
spike may not behave like native bound material.
:::

::: {#hint-explore .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hints E1–E4"}
Changing sample allocation changes the weighting of a pooled average. In the
extraction experiment, keep total solvent fixed; every portion is fresh, phases
equilibrate and are separated completely in this ideal model.
:::

::: {#hint-r1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R1"}
The raw table contains four grabs from each equal-mass stratum. Balanced counts
make the arithmetic coincide. Unequal counts generally break that coincidence.
:::

::: {#hint-r2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R2"}
mg/L × L gives mg, then mg/g uses original sample grams. The final flask and
original solid do not have interchangeable concentration units.
:::

::: {#hint-r3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R3"}
Use $(1.50\times10/1)\times0.04000/0.4000$ and identify which losses are assumed
absent. The formula alone does not demonstrate them absent.
:::

::: {#hint-r4 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R4"}
[`group_by()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/group_by.html) separates
stratum summaries. An unsampled stratum has unknown concentration, not a measured
zero. A bulk estimate needs its evidence or a justified model.
:::

## Solutions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions B1–B5"}
**B1.** $(8+14+25)/3=15.667$ mg/kg. Top-only sampling approaches 8 mg/kg. A small
repeat SD describes the top measurements, not the bias from excluding other
material.

**B2.** $0.50(8)+0.30(14)+0.20(25)=13.2$ mg/kg. Equal weights would represent
three equal masses that no longer exist in this new target.

**B3.** Final-to-extract factor $10/2=5$ gives 9.60 mg/L extract. Amount is
$9.60\times0.02500=0.240$ mg; divided by 0.5000 g it gives 0.480 mg/g extracted.

**B4.** One recovery $1-20/110=0.81818$; two recoveries together give
$1-(20/65)^2=0.90533$. This assumes constant distribution ratio and phase volumes,
equilibrium, complete separation and fresh solvent for each extraction, with no
reaction or handling loss. It is not validation of real native extraction.

**B5.** No. The late spike tests incremental behaviour after it was added, not
native analyte lost before addition. A native bound analyte can differ from a
freely dissolved spike, so equivalence also needs evidence.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions E1–E4"}
**E1.** With equal grab counts, the two averages agree. Twenty top plus three
middle and three bottom grabs make the naive average target
$(20\times8+3\times14+3\times25)/26=10.654$ mg/kg in expectation. The average of
the three stratum means remains near 15.667 mg/kg and uses the supplied mass
weights. Exact simulated results vary with run.

**E2.** The full bulk quantity cannot be estimated from all strata by this
procedure because middle and bottom are absent. Top-only precision cannot
supply their concentrations. The demo withholds the stratified estimate rather
than inventing zeros.

**E3.** The realised grabs and estimated means vary. The defined equal-mass target
and the rule for weighting strata remain fixed. More independent grabs reduce
random variation under this model but do not justify a different sampling target.

**E4.** Recoveries are 81.8% and 90.5%. Lower D leaves more analyte in the aqueous
phase. Several fresh extractions improve this ideal equilibrium recovery, but
bound analyte, reaction, emulsion, incomplete equilibration or handling loss can
invalidate the ideal assumptions.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions R1–R4"}
**R1.** Supplied stratum means are 8, 14 and 25 mg/kg. Equal counts and equal
stratum masses make the pooled mean equal the equal-stratum mean. The three
caffeine results are 0.480, 0.490 and 0.750 mg/g. Recovery calculations match B4.

**R2.** `/1000` converts extract mL into L. `extract_mg_l` refers to the extract;
`extracted_mg` is amount in its total volume; `caffeine_mg_g` refers to original
solid mass. Reporting 1.92 mg/L final as 1.92 mg/g confuses quantities and ignores
the preparation chain.

**R3.** $1.50\times10=15.0$ mg/L extract; $15.0\times0.04000=0.600$ mg;
$0.600/0.4000=1.50$ mg/g extracted. This still assumes valid measured concentration
and no transfer loss, and does not establish complete native recovery.

**R4.** R reproduces the demo's all-grab mean and equal mean of stratum means
when all three strata appear. Missing rows for a stratum mean it was not sampled.
Replacing that missing evidence with zero would create a false bulk estimate.
:::

## Where this leads

[Error and uncertainty](../error-uncertainty/exercise.qmd) separates variability
from bias and asks which uncertainty sources a set of repeat readings can
actually estimate. In later methods, keep the original material basis when
undoing aliquot, extract and dilution steps.
